title: The bot restarted. How does it know what it already did?
author: Electrical_Waltz_888
selftext:
Here’s a test I’d run before trusting an automated system: restart it while a position is open.

Say the bot bought 50 shares before it crashed. The broker still shows 50 shares and a working stop. The bot comes back up with an empty local state, and the entry signal is still true.

If it goes straight back to scanning, it could treat that same signal as a fresh entry. The strategy didn’t change. The bot just forgot what it had already done.

I’d ask AI to turn the restart into a test case: “List what the bot needs to confirm about positions, working orders and previously processed signals before it can resume. If it can’t establish any of those, say what remains unknown.”

What does your system do on restart if its own records disagree with the broker: pause, rebuild its state, or hand it back to you?

Disclosure: I wrote *The Complete Guide to AI Powered Trading*  It includes worked examples and 50 reusable prompts for writing trading rules, questioning backtest results and reviewing trades with AI.

[Find the book on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0HNM97TQ9)

comments.author: Ok_Map5721
comments.body:
Ran into exactly this with my own bot. What I ended up with:

The exchange is the source of truth, never the local state. On startup the bot pulls open positions and working orders first, before it's allowed to look at a single signal. If the local record agrees, it resumes. If they disagree, it doesn't guess. It cancels nothing, opens nothing, logs the mismatch and pauses until I look at it. A paused bot costs a missed trade. A bot that "fixes" things on its own can double a position.

Two smaller things that helped:  
\- A client order ID built from the signal (symbol + bar timestamp + side). If the bot restarts and tries to send the same order again, the exchange rejects the duplicate instead of filling it twice.  
\- A cooldown after any exit or restart before re-entry is allowed. Otherwise the same still-true signal fires again on the next bar.

Testing it the way you describe is the right call. Kill the process mid-trade on testnet a few times and check what it does on the way back up.

replies.author: Electrical_Waltz_888
replies.body:
Pausing on a mismatch makes sense. Missing an entry is easier to deal with than discovering the bot doubled a position while trying to recover.

The restart case I’d test next is when the exchange accepts and fills the order, but the bot dies before it receives the acknowledgement. On restart there’s no working order to find. Do you check recent fills against the client order ID as well, or does the position mismatch send it straight to manual review?

replies.author: Ok_Map5721
replies.body:
Good case, and the one that actually bites in practice. The way I'd handle it: write the intent down before sending anything. The bot saves a small journal entry (client order ID, side, size, signal time) to disk first, then sends the order.

On restart, every journal entry without a confirmed result gets looked up on the exchange by its client order ID. Most exchanges let you query by client ID even after the order is filled, and the trade history has it too. Then:

\- Found and filled: the position mismatch is explained, record the fill and resume  
\- Found, partially filled or still working: adopt it as is, don't send a new one  
\- Not found at all: the order never reached the exchange, safe to treat as not sent

Only a mismatch the journal can't explain goes to manual review. That keeps the common case (died between send and ack) automatic, and leaves the human for the genuinely weird stuff, like a position that appears with no intent behind it.

One catch: check how long your exchange keeps order history searchable by client ID. If the bot can be down longer than that window, the lookup can come back empty and look like "never sent" when it wasn't.
